strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly identifies and addresses the limitation of finite surrogate regret bounds in non-stationary settings with compelling examples
Tight theoretical results: Provides both upper bounds (Theorems 3.4, 4.5) and matching lower bounds (Theorem 5.1), demonstrating tightness of the dependence on FT and PT
Technical quality: Rigorous proofs, correct synthesis of dynamic regret analysis with surrogate gap exploitation, and novel technical lemmas for convolutional Fenchel-Young losses
Generality: Extends from settings with Ŷ = Y (prior work) to problems with Ŷ ≠ Y, addressing important structured prediction tasks like label ranking with NDCG loss
Methodological contribution: Polyak-style learning rate automatically provides target-loss guarantees and shows promising empirical performance in non-stationary settings
Generalization of OGD analysis: Proposition 2.4 properly extends Zinkevich's dynamic regret to non-increasing learning rates, which may be of independent interest
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental validation: Only binary classification experiments comparing learning rates in Appendix E; no experiments on main problems (multiclass, multilabel, label ranking) or evidence that FT and PT are small in practice

Impractical learning rate computation: Implementing ηt in (4) requires evaluating Eyˆt∼π(θt)[ℓ(ŷt, yt)] via Frank-Wolfe algorithms at each round; computational overhead is claimed but not experimentally validated
Full-information feedback restriction: Practical applicability limited to settings with full label revelation; bandit feedback settings explicitly excluded with no proposed solution

Unclear practical significance: While theoretically improved over fixed-comparator bounds, no evidence that improvements translate to realistic scenarios; constants MD/α and D/2 can be large and problem-dependent
Incremental novelty: Core techniques (dynamic regret, surrogate gap) exist separately in prior work; main contribution is their combination for non-stationary structured prediction

Incomplete presentation of technical details: Learning rate condition (4) is complex without sufficient intuition; necessity of the min(·, ηt−1) operation in (5) underexplained; Section 4.2 lacks intuition for Lemmas 4.3 and 4.4
No reproducibility support: No code provided; Frank-Wolfe implementation details for π(θt) computation are non-trivial; limited guidance for practitioners
Missing baseline comparisons: No comparison against alternative approaches, fixed comparators, or simpler methods; no ablation studies

strengths: Clear problem formulation with well-motivated non-stationary setting and intuitive examples (e.g., label flips) showing when prior bounds fail
Technically sound proofs with complete development; clean synthesis of dynamic regret analysis with surrogate gap technique
Extension to convolutional Fenchel-Young losses (Section 4) with new technical lemmas (4.3, 4.4) handling broader problem classes including label ranking with different label and prediction sets
Complementary lower bound (Theorem 5.1) demonstrating tight dependence on F_T and P_T
Generalizes prior finite surrogate regret bounds and provides framework applicable to any comparator sequence
weaknesses: Limited core technical novelty: the main contribution (combining Zinkevich's dynamic regret bounds with surrogate gap technique) is incremental; the authors acknowledge Van der Hoeven et al. [32] previously mentioned this possibility but did not work out the bounds

Severely insufficient experimental validation: only toy synthetic experiments (2D binary classification with label flips); no real-world datasets, no comparison with other online learning methods, no demonstration of practical utility; experiments only validate heuristic learning rate, not theoretical results

Restrictive assumptions especially in Section 3: Assumption 3.1 requires Ŷ = Y and affine decomposability; Assumption 3.2 (surrogate gap) is specific to certain decoding methods; applicability unclear before reading Section 4

Questionable practical applicability: requires choosing comparator sequences in advance (problem-dependent), learning rate is only a feasible range with heuristic rule (Eq. 5) validated only on toys, computing decoding distribution expectations adds overhead with no real-world validation
Minimal comparison with concurrent work: Boudart et al. [8] independently studied non-stationary online structured prediction; relationship and relative merits insufficiently discussed

strengths: Clear and compelling motivation: The paper effectively motivates why previous surrogate regret bounds fail in non-stationary settings through the label-flip example, demonstrating how the proposed small-surrogate-loss + path-length bound achieves O(1) vs Ω(T).

Elegant theoretical approach: The core insight of designing a learning rate with lower bound (α/M) ensuring feasibility and upper bound enabling loss cancellation is simple yet effective, cleanly synthesizing dynamic regret analysis with surrogate gap exploitation.

Generality and breadth of applicability: The work encompasses Fenchel-Young losses (Section 3) and extends to convolutional Fenchel-Young losses for problems with Y ≠ Ŷ (Section 4), enabling coverage of important problems like NDCG ranking loss.
Tight theoretical characterization: Theorem 5.1 proves both linear dependence on FT and PT are necessary, providing a complete theoretical picture.

Practical contribution: The Polyak-style learning rate (Eq. 5) naturally emerges from theory, admits efficient computation via Carathéodory's theorem, and empirically outperforms baselines under high non-stationarity.

Technical soundness: Proofs are correct and non-obvious, with novel lemmas (4.3-4.4) introducing target-surrogate relations and auxiliary loss lower bounds appropriately adapted from Cao et al. [10] to the online setting.

Clear exposition: Well-organized presentation with strong motivation, main results before details, comprehensive appendices, and careful discussion of prior work including critique of hinge loss issues.
weaknesses: Limited experimental validation: Only synthetic binary classification experiments (Appendix E) on label-flip scenarios; no real-world datasets, no comparison with competing methods, no ablation studies. For theory paper this is acceptable but Polyak-style learning rate's practical utility claims lack strong empirical support.

Restriction to full-information feedback: Significant limitation acknowledged by authors; extension to bandit feedback is posed as unclear future work. Limits practical applicability in domains where only partial feedback is available.

Computational and practical concerns inadequately addressed: Computing Polyak-style rate requires sampling from π(θt) and evaluating expectations at each step; while polynomial in d, this requires solving optimization problems per round (Frank-Wolfe, etc.). Bound constants (e.g., c = MD(α^{-1}D/2 + PT)) could be large but no empirical analysis provided.

Incomplete novelty assessment: Core technique (combining dynamic regret with surrogate gap) is relatively straightforward once formulated; heavy reliance on recent work (Cao et al. [10], Sakaue et al. [28]) suggests incremental rather than fundamental innovation.

Lower bound limited in scope: Theorem 5.1 only establishes tightness for binary classification with smooth hinge loss; doesn't rule out better bounds for specific problem classes or provide tight bounds under other assumptions.

Restrictive assumptions: Assumption 3.1 (affine decomposability with specific geometric properties) requires particular problem structure; Assumption 3.2 (surrogate gap) requires randomized decoding non-trivial to verify; Assumption 3.3 (self-bounding) excludes some convex losses.

Incomplete treatment of concurrent work: Boudart et al. [8] addressed non-stationary online structured prediction independently; paper notes different metrics but lacks thorough comparison of implications for practitioners.

Presentation gaps: Motivation for extending to convolutional Fenchel-Young losses (Section 4) unclear; computational cost of decoding distributions discussed only at high level; no analysis of when bounds are tight vs. loose in practice.

strengths: Addresses fundamental limitation of prior work: finite surrogate regret bounds fail under non-stationarity. The label-flip example (Figure 1) clearly motivates the problem.

Clean and elegant theoretical approach: combines dynamic regret analysis (Proposition 2.4) with surrogate gap exploitation using clever learning rate design (Eq. 4) that enables cancellation of cumulative surrogate loss terms.
Theoretically complete: provides matching upper (Theorems 3.4, 4.5) and lower bounds (Theorem 5.1), proving tight dependence on F_T and P_T.

Extends to new problem classes: Section 4's use of convolutional Fenchel–Young losses handles important settings where label and prediction sets differ (e.g., ranking with NDCG loss), which prior work couldn't handle.
Novel technical contributions: Lemmas 4.3 and 4.4 establish new target–surrogate relationships for convolutional Fenchel–Young losses with potential broader utility.

Well-motivated practical algorithm: Polyak-style learning rate (Eq. 5) derived from analysis shows consistent improvements over constant and AdaGrad learning rates, especially under high non-stationarity (Appendix E).

Excellent presentation: clear problem motivation, well-organized sections, comprehensive appendices with detailed proofs, examples, and discussion of related work limitations (Appendix C on hinge loss).
weaknesses: Severely limited feedback model: restricted to full-information feedback. Extension to bandit/limited feedback is acknowledged as open, significantly limiting practical applicability. Most real systems require partial feedback.

Learning rate computation complexity: Equation (4) requires computing E[ℓ(ŷ_t, y_t)] via randomized decoding and solving optimization problems (e.g., Eq. 9 for ranking). While claimed to be O(d²) oracle calls, this is non-trivial to implement and overhead versus simpler methods is unclear.

Hidden large constants: bounds depend on problem-dependent parameters (MD/α in Thm 3.4, D/λ in Thm 4.5). For K-class classification, α = 1/K yields linear scaling with K. No empirical study of whether these constants are reasonable in practice.

Limited experimental validation: only synthetic 2D and MNIST 3-class experiments. No evaluation on realistic structured prediction tasks (actual ranking, NLP problems). Experiments relegated to appendix; main paper lacks empirical grounding. No comparison with concurrent non-stationary methods (Boudart et al. 2024).

Practical path length requirement unclear: bounds' utility depends on keeping P_T small, which requires choosing comparators wisely. This is non-trivial since the full environment isn't known in advance, limiting practical guidance.

Assumption complexity persists: Section 3 still requires Assumption 3.1 (affine decomposability, label encoding separation, etc.); Section 4 requires Assumption 4.2 on Ω. Applicability to general structured prediction problems remains unclear.
Incomplete comparisons: relationship to Boudart et al. (2024) not thoroughly discussed; no quantitative comparison of constants between Theorems 3.4 and 4.5 to guide practitioners.
